clue.text: Doubting it with number reversed in account

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so an outer piece surrounds the rest

parts.note: AC is the standard abbreviation for account

indicators.note: something reversed is turned back to front, so the letters are read from the other end

parts.note: taken as written
a number is a song in a musical performance

explanation.surface: Someone sceptical about a figure that was entered backwards in a ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is a song, not a digit, which is the trap in a clue about accounts; AC is the usual abbreviation for account.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnostic holds that God's existence cannot be known, so the word describes a doubting, uncommitted religious outlook.

clue.text: Cool flower excited Gaelic Romeo

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An Irish or Scottish lover, laid-back and flushed with excitement, presents someone with a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is not a bloom but a thing that flows, and a slow river of ice is certainly cool.
explanation.definitionFit: A glacier is a mass of ice moving slowly downhill, so it is a cold thing that flows.

clue.text: Greek character old and enormous

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
mega is slang for huge

explanation.surface: A figure from Greek legend who is ancient and gigantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in a story; here it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, and letters are called characters in writing systems.

clue.text: Slept so badly without so much as a bra?

definitions.text: without so much as a bra?

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in a disordered arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who had a restless night because they went to bed wearing nothing up top.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition by example: going braless is one way of being uncovered above the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: Topless means bare above the waist, and wearing not even a bra is the obvious case of it.

clue.text: An Earnshaw in renovated yacht?

indicators.note: a renovated thing has been rebuilt and remade, so the letters are rebuilt into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A member of a family spotted aboard a refitted boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earnshaws are the family at the heart of Wuthering Heights, one of the puzzle's themes.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine Earnshaw, called Cathy, is the heroine of Emily Bronte's novel and daughter of the Earnshaw household.

clue.text: See 23
Online writer, second-rate feller

parts.note: B grade is second class
a logger fells trees, so he is literally a feller

explanation.surface: An internet author dismissed as a mediocre bloke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feller' reads as slang for a man, but here it is one who fells trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A blogger writes posts for a website, so the person is an author who publishes on the internet.

clue.text: Beer wasted in population leaving London?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: liquid that slops over the rim of a glass and is lost
second meaning: people rehoused from a crowded city into new towns

explanation.surface: Pints being spilt among the crowds moving out of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: After the Second World War, London's excess population was moved to new towns, and planners called those people the city's overspill; the question mark admits London is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both liquid that has run over the edge of a container and surplus residents relocated from a congested city.

clue.text: Time locks securing home: into this one might vanish

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: locks are tresses of hair
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Timed locks on a house seem to make things disappear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' are tresses, not bolts, and being 'in' is a common way of saying at home.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish into thin air is an idiom for disappearing completely without trace.

clue.text: Singer to tempt Ham's boy, as Spooner says

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

parts.note: to tempt is to BAIT; it takes the opening sound of the second word
Cush is a son of Ham, son of Noah, in Genesis; it takes the opening sound of the first word

explanation.surface: A singer being lured by a biblical figure's son.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first sounds of BAIT CUSH and you get the singer. She had a hit with Wuthering Heights, which ties her to the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Kate Bush is an English singer-songwriter whose 1978 debut single retold Emily Bronte's novel.

clue.text: Still around at hospital, melon variety causing illness

indicators.note: to be around something is to encircle it, so one word wraps round the others

parts.note: a still is a photograph, a pic
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hospital
the Ogen is a variety of melon

explanation.surface: A patient still in hospital because a type of melon made them sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is a noun, a photo, not an adverb meaning yet; the Ogen is a small green-fleshed melon bred in Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathogenic describes microbes or agents capable of producing disease in a host organism.

clue.text: Motorway madness an illusion?

parts.note: the M1, written MI in crosswords, is Britain's main north-south motorway
rage is fury or madness

explanation.surface: Wondering whether road rage on the highway is all in the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords treat the M1 motorway as MI, reading the digit one as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical effect such as shimmering water seen in a desert, a trick of the eye.

clue.text: On top, man turned against former European

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: on top of that means also, in addition
a guy is a man
V, versus, means against

explanation.surface: Having gained the upper hand, a man turns on a fellow from a country that no longer exists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top' reads as winning; it means 'as well', as in 'on top of that'. The reversal covers both words before it, and V for versus follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s, so a Yugoslav is a citizen of a European state that has gone.

clue.text: Sweet thing to quarrel trashing snug in pub

indicators.note: placed in something means sitting inside it, so the other letters go within

parts.note: a bar is a pub
a row is a quarrel

indicators.note: trashing something wrecks it, so its letters are smashed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sweetheart picks a fight by wrecking the cosy back room of a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A snug is a small private room in a British pub, which makes it look like part of the scene rather than letters to scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown sugar is a sweetener, partly refined with molasses left in, so it is a sweet substance.

clue.text: Rowing with Hunger (Boat Race book)

parts.note: surface reading: the title of a sports memoir about oarsmen straining in a race
setter's reading: a spoof title for a classic novel full of rowing in the sense of bitter quarrels, and of hungry, obsessive passion

explanation.walkthrough: Rowing here means arguing, and hunger means desperate longing; together they sum up Emily Bronte's novel, which Kate Bush also turned into a song.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bronte novel is dominated by feuds between families and Heathcliff's consuming desire for Cathy, so the joke title fits the book.

clue.text: State aim ultimately denied

indicators.note: the ultimate part is the end, and denying it means taking it away

parts.note: a goal is an aim

explanation.surface: A government is refused what it was ultimately aiming for.
explanation.walkthrough: GOAL loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Goa is a small coastal state on the west coast of India, formerly Portuguese.

clue.text: Nitrogen in unopened pickle is concerning

indicators.note: not opened means its front is still shut away, so the first letter goes
one thing in another is held inside it

parts.note: a pickle is a mess, a mire; without its first letter it becomes IRE
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: Nitrogen in a jar of pickles that has never been opened is worrying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickle' means a predicament, a MIRE, not a gherkin; beheaded it is IRE, with N placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: In re is Latin legal phrasing used in letters and documents meaning about or on the subject of.

clue.text: Try small drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an attempt, as in have a go
second meaning: a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: An invitation to sample a little something to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' looks like a verb inviting a taste; it is the noun for an attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an attempt at something and a single small measure of liquor served in a glass.

clue.text: See 14
Tortured character has passion to steal back female

parts.note: heat is intense passion

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run from the end

parts.note: to filch is to pilfer
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A tormented man whose desire drives him to snatch a woman back.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair summary of the novel's plot, which makes it hard to see the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Heathcliff is the brooding, anguished antihero of Wuthering Heights, a figure driven by love and revenge.

clue.text: Encourage judge in that case to release husband

parts.note: a judge hears a case

indicators.note: releasing something lets it go, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: then means in that case
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Urging a judge to free a husband from the case in front of him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In that case' looks like courtroom language but simply means THEN, which loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten is to give someone courage or cheer, so the verb matches the sense of encourage.

clue.text: Weapon to keep animals together outside a pound

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the others

parts.note: to herd is to keep animals in a group
taken as written
LB is the abbreviation for pound weight

explanation.surface: A weapon used for keeping livestock penned inside a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: A pound is also an animal enclosure, which suits the herding surface; here it is the weight LB.
explanation.definitionFit: A halberd is a medieval pole arm combining a spear point and an axe blade, a fighting implement.

clue.text: Bridge manoeuvre punishes opponents

parts.note: to fine is to punish with a penalty
South and East sit on opposite sides at the bridge table

explanation.surface: A clever play at the card table that penalises the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge North-South play against East-West, so any pair such as S and E are opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: A finesse in bridge is an attempt to win a trick with a lower card, hoping an opponent holds the higher one.

clue.text: Dog in show with energy chewed lead

parts.note: to air something is to show it publicly

indicators.note: chewed things are mangled by teeth, so the letters are mashed into a new order

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lively dog at a dog show gnaws through its leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' and 'lead' both belong to the dog-show picture; AIR comes from show as a verb, and E joins LEAD to be scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: The Airedale is a large terrier breed that originated in a Yorkshire valley, so it is a dog.

clue.text: Writer's initially outrageous liberty grated with men

indicators.note: grated food is shredded into bits, so the letters are broken up and reset
initially means at the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer took a shocking liberty that got on the nerves of the men around her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grated' reads as annoyed; it is the signal to shred the letters. The 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Bronte was the English novelist and poet who wrote Wuthering Heights, published in 1847.

clue.text: Deplore unconvincing book collection

parts.note: a lame excuse is an unconvincing one
NT, the New Testament, is a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Complaining about a feeble library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book collection' suggests a library; it is the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament is to express sorrow or regret over something, a close verb synonym of deplore.

clue.text: Sennett's Normand married Magwitch?

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
Abel Magwitch is the convict in Dickens's Great Expectations

explanation.surface: A silent-film comedienne wed to a Dickens convict.
explanation.walkthrough: Mabel Normand was the star of Mack Sennett's silent comedies; the surname Magwitch leads to his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mack Sennett's leading comic actress was Mabel Normand, so her first name is the one wanted.

clue.text: Embracing one, this clerk surprisingly virtuous?

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so the other letters wrap round a piece
a surprising outcome is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An office clerk who hugs a colleague and turns out, unexpectedly, to be a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by extreme example: being like Christ is the height of virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Christlike means showing the qualities of Jesus, such as goodness and self-sacrifice, a supreme form of righteousness.

clue.text: See 9
Figure is round, not entirely lifeless

indicators.note: not the entire thing means part is missing, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: taken as written
O is round in shape
gone means dead

explanation.surface: A plump body that is still just about alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' and 'round' suggest a body shape; the figure is geometric. GONE loses its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: An isogon is a polygon with all its angles equal, a shape in geometry.

clue.text: Caller out to engage occasionally good Swiss singer?

indicators.note: to engage is to take on or hold, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: one who calls out loudly is a yeller

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is taken

parts.note: every second letter of the word

explanation.surface: A shouter is hired to take on a fairly decent Alpine vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is by example: yodelling is the singing style associated with the Swiss Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: Yodelling is the traditional Alpine vocal style, so a yodeller is the stereotypical Swiss performer.
